sections.html:
Peabody is an Essex County city on the North Shore, about 15 miles northeast of Boston and 2 miles from the center of Salem. It covers 16.81 square miles, shaped like a wedge, with the center at the wider northeastern end. South Peabody lies below the center, and the more suburban West Peabody, where the high school sits, is out past the highways and the Proctor neighborhood. Middleton, Danvers, Salem, Lynn and Lynnfield border it.

The 2020 census counted 54,481 residents in 22,315 households and 23,191 housing units, with 3.8% of units vacant. The population doubled between 1950 and 1970, from 22,645 to 48,080, so a large share of homes date from that postwar growth. About 24.2% of residents are 65 or older, and older owners and estates are a steady source of local sales.

Property classFY26 rate
Residential$9.47
Commercial$18.85

The city sets rates each fiscal year. Check the unit and your own bill with the assessors, since the bill is the final word on what you owe.

The Assessors Office page also links to a cyclical inspection program FAQ, property value information, real estate exemptions and a Property Tax 101 guide.

Call the assessors at 978-538-5716. Before a sale, ask two things. Does an exemption on your bill end when the property transfers? And does the cyclical inspection program have a visit scheduled for your address? A pending inspection can change the record on your house, and a buyer may ask about it.

Share the current bill with any buyer's attorney so closing adjustments make sense, and ask the assessors how an exemption you hold is treated after the transfer.

The Ipswich River forms the northwestern border, and the Waters River drains the northeast. Low-lying lots near those waterways deserve a flood question before you sell, so check your status with your insurer and the city building office and write down anything you know about wet basements.

Peabody has useful green space that buyers often ask about: Independence Greenway, a 5.25 mile rail trail, and Brooksby Farm, a 275-acre city-owned farm and conservation area. Crystal Lake, a 21-acre conservation area, is another local landmark. If your house sits in a designated historic district, such as the Washington Street Historic District, ask the city whether any local rules apply.

sections.h2: Older houses and what buyers check
sections.html:
Peabody was settled in 1626 as part of Salem and became a city in 1916. Leather made the city's name for generations, and it is still called the Leather City, but the tanneries have closed or moved. A big share of the housing was added during the postwar boom, when the population doubled in twenty years.

Houses of similar age tend to need the same work at about the same time: roofs, boilers, wiring and windows. A buyer's inspector will list those items, and a lender may ask for repairs before it releases funds. That is the situation where owners weigh an as-is sale against a repair project. West Peabody, mostly farm land until the 1950s, has newer houses than the area around the center, so age and condition vary by section.

The Peabody Municipal Light Plant, owned by the city, provides electricity, so transferring electric service to a new owner runs through a city utility, which is different from most Massachusetts towns. National Grid supplies natural gas, and Comcast and RCN hold cable licenses.

Highways include Interstate 95, Route 128, Route 129, U.S. Route 1 and Route 114. Several MBTA bus lines pass through town. There is no commuter rail station in the city, and the closest stop is in Salem on the Newburyport/Rockport Line to North Station. The nearest airports are Beverly Municipal and Boston's Logan.

Start with the fire department. A Peabody seller needs an alarm certificate, and state fire officials advise calling for the inspection as soon as a closing date exists and expecting a fee. The Department of Fire Services explains the steps.

An attorney handles the closing and the recorded deed, since attorneys are part of Massachusetts sales by law and by practice. The deed excise is set by Chapter 64D, Section 1. Sellers of certain residential properties also cannot make an offer conditional on a waiver of a home inspection under 760 CMR 74.

A direct purchase follows the same legal path. You may still need to clear a mortgage payoff, estate paperwork or a lien before the deed records.

sections.h2: Order of work for a Peabody sale
sections.html:
A sale moves faster when you do the slow items first.

  • Request your tax and assessment information from the assessors and note any exemption.
  • Find your home's build date and last permit date, then check the age of every smoke and carbon monoxide alarm.
  • Set a closing date and call the fire department for the inspection, expecting a fee.
  • Ask your lender for a payoff figure if a mortgage remains, and collect estate paperwork if heirs are selling.
  • Give everything to your attorney, who handles the closing and the recorded deed.

If the house is in the Washington Street Historic District or another designated area, add one more call to the city about local rules before you commit to repairs or a closing date.

Buyers describe Peabody by section, so use those names in your description.

  • The center and Peabody Square in the northeast.
  • South Peabody, with Tillie's Farm, a city-owned farm.
  • West Peabody, home to the high school.
  • The Proctor neighborhood between the center and the west.

West Peabody was mostly farm land until the 1950s and has since grown into a residential area, so houses there tend to be newer than those near the center.

Whichever section you are in, name it clearly when you talk to buyers, and mention the nearest highway access and bus lines, since commuters to Boston make up much of the local market. Ask your agent or attorney about parking and access too.

sections.h2: When a cash sale makes sense
sections.html:
A cash sale can fit when you want a firm closing date and do not want to prepare a house for the market. The legal steps stay the same: the fire department certificate, a payoff for any mortgage and a deed recorded at the registry.

  • Estates in which heirs live out of state.
  • Houses needing roof, heating or electrical work.
  • Owners facing a move on a short schedule.

Tell us what the house needs and who has to sign, and we can describe how an offer would line up with those documents. Before you call, gather the deed, the latest tax bill, any payoff letter and, for an estate, the paperwork showing who has authority. With those in hand the closing timeline gets shorter, and you can compare the offer with the cost and delay of repairs and showings.

faqs.q: What are Peabody's property tax rates?
faqs.a: The FY26 rates are $9.47 residential and $18.85 commercial, Check the unit and your own bill with the assessors.

faqs.q: Who do I call about Peabody property assessments?
faqs.a: Call the Assessors Office at 978-538-5716. Its page also links to exemption information and a cyclical inspection FAQ.

faqs.q: Does Peabody run its own electric utility?
faqs.a: Yes. The city-owned Peabody Municipal Light Plant provides electricity, while National Grid provides natural gas.

faqs.q: Is there commuter rail in Peabody?
faqs.a: No station is in the city. The nearest commuter rail service is in Salem on the Newburyport/Rockport Line.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Peabody?
faqs.a: Yes. A sale needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the alarms meet requirements.
